question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Sequence of Dutch withdrawal from Indian subcontinent territories]
options: Nagapattinam — Lost to the British in 1781 (formally 1784)
Cochin — Lost to the British in 1795
Chinsurah (Chinsura) — Dutch factory on the Hooghly River in Bengal
Masulipatnam — Last Dutch possession in India, retained until 1825
wrong_fact: Masulipatnam was not the last Dutch possession retained until 1825. Chinsurah (on the Hooghly River, Bengal) was the last Dutch foothold in India, exchanged with the British in 1825 under the Treaty of London for Bencoolen (Sumatra). Masulipatnam had been abandoned much earlier.
explanation: The Dutch progressively withdrew from India: Nagapattinam (1781/1784), Cochin (1795), and finally Chinsurah (Chinsura) on the Hooghly in Bengal — which was swapped with Britain for Bencoolen in Sumatra under the Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824 (effected 1825). Masulipatnam was not the last Dutch foothold; Chinsurah was.

question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824 and territorial exchanges]
options: Chinsurah — Dutch enclave on the Hooghly River ceded to Britain
Bencoolen (Bengkulu) — British settlement in Sumatra given to the Dutch
Malacca — British returned Malacca to the Dutch under the 1824 Treaty
Singapore — Confirmed as a British possession under the 1824 Treaty, free from Dutch claims
wrong_fact: Malacca was NOT returned to the Dutch under the 1824 Treaty; quite the opposite. Under the Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824 (Treaty of London), Britain received Malacca from the Dutch (along with Bangka Island) in exchange for Bencoolen and other settlements in Sumatra. Malacca thus became British, not Dutch.
explanation: The Treaty of London (1824) was a major reorganisation: Britain got Malacca (confirmed), Singapore, and Chinsurah; the Dutch got Bencoolen and British interests in Sumatra. Far from returning Malacca to the Dutch, Britain permanently acquired it. Singapore was confirmed as British, settling the dispute over Raffles' 1819 founding. This treaty essentially divided Malay world between Britain (north of the Strait) and Netherlands (south).

question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Dutch withdrawal from South and Southeast Asia and the reorientation of Dutch colonial focus]
options: Java — Remained the heartland of the Dutch colonial empire (Dutch East Indies) after withdrawal from India
Batavia (Jakarta) — Continued as the capital of the Dutch East Indies after loss of Indian territories
Aceh (Sumatra) — Dutch fought a prolonged war here in the late 19th century to consolidate Indonesian control
Malabar Coast — Dutch retained significant trading rights here through the Dutch Malabar Convention of 1825
wrong_fact: There was no 'Dutch Malabar Convention of 1825' granting retained trading rights on the Malabar Coast. After losing Cochin in 1795 and formally in 1814, the Dutch had no significant presence or treaty rights on the Malabar Coast. Dutch colonial reorientation post-1825 focused entirely on the Indonesian archipelago.
explanation: After their Indian withdrawal, Dutch colonial energies refocused on Java (with Batavia as capital) and consolidating control over the Indonesian archipelago. The Aceh War (1873–1904) was a real, prolonged Dutch military campaign in northern Sumatra. However, no 'Dutch Malabar Convention of 1825' existed — the Dutch had completely withdrawn from the Malabar Coast by 1814–1825 with no retained trading rights.
